# Electrode-selection study (supplementary, post-test; generated by scripts/analyze_selection_study.py)

Question: can another rule pick better electrode subsets than the frozen relevance rule? Each method chose 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16 electrodes, and EEGNet was trained on each subset with the frozen recipe on all of session 1 (the training day), then scored once on session 2 (the held-out day). 1350 new runs; 135 earlier runs supply relevance at 8, 10, 12 and 16 electrodes and all 22 electrodes (results/test and the electrode-count sweep, same recipe and seeds).

The methods, in plain words:

- relevance (frozen rule): scores each electrode on its own, by how well its band power separates the classes.
- Riemannian distance: keeps the subset whose class-average covariance matrices (how electrodes vary together) stay farthest apart.
- CSP patterns: ranks electrodes by their weight in the common spatial patterns that best separate each class from the rest.
- wrapper: drops electrodes one at a time, each time the one whose loss a fast surrogate decoder (tangent space + logistic regression) notices least, judged by cross-validation over session-1 runs.
- learned: a concrete (Gumbel-softmax) selector trained end to end in front of EEGNet, one per count.
- physiology prior: a fixed order around C3, C4 and Cz, the classic hand and foot sites; uses no data.
- population (pop-*): one montage for a new user, from the average rank of each electrode over the other eight participants' relevance, Riemannian or wrapper rankings.

## What this can and cannot show

- Every ranking and subset was chosen from session 1 only. The population montages of a participant use only the other eight participants' session-1 rankings, never that participant's own data.
- The session-2 numbers are exploratory: this study was planned after the main study's test results were known, so it is not a test of a hypothesis fixed in advance, and it does not replace the frozen final configuration (relevance-16-prune50, INT8).
- Nine participants. An interval that contains zero does not show that two methods are equal, and none of this shows how new people would fare.

## How to read the numbers

Accuracy is the share of artifact-free session-2 trials classified correctly (four classes, chance 25%). Each participant's accuracy is the mean of seeds 0, 1, 2; tables give the mean of the nine participants. Differences are in percentage points (pp), written as mean [95% interval] better/worse: the interval resamples the nine participants (10,000 bootstrap resamples, seed 690), and better/worse counts the participants whose accuracy is higher/lower (the rest are tied).

## Highest mean at each count

| electrodes | highest mean | accuracy % | minus relevance (pp) | minus all 22 (pp) |
| ---: | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| 4 | wrapper (surrogate decoder) | 58.9 | +3.9 [-0.1, +8.3] 6/3 | -6.2 [-9.4, -3.1] 0/9 |
| 6 | Riemannian distance | 62.7 | +4.0 [+0.6, +7.5] 6/3 | -2.4 [-5.3, +1.2] 1/8 |
| 8 | Riemannian distance | 64.3 | +4.4 [+2.0, +7.0] 8/1 | -0.7 [-3.6, +2.2] 4/5 |
| 10 | physiology prior | 64.6 | +3.2 [+1.3, +5.2] 8/1 | -0.5 [-2.0, +1.0] 4/5 |
| 12 | wrapper (surrogate decoder) | 64.4 | +1.2 [-0.5, +3.1] 5/4 | -0.6 [-3.7, +2.2] 3/6 |
| 16 | relevance (frozen rule) | 66.2 | (this is the relevance rule) | +1.2 [-1.3, +3.7] 6/3 |

Picking the highest of 9 means after the fact favours a lucky method. There are 48 comparisons with relevance; if no method truly differed, roughly one in twenty intervals would still exclude zero by chance, so one such interval on its own is weak evidence.

## The wrapper's own estimate on the training day

The wrapper chose its subsets by the cross-validated accuracy of a fast surrogate decoder on session 1. Next to it, EEGNet trained on the same subset and scored on session 2. The two use different decoders and days, so compare how each changes with the count, not the levels.

| electrodes | surrogate decoder, session-1 cross-validation % | EEGNet, session 2 % |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 22 | 67.0 | 65.0 |
| 16 | 69.7 | 64.9 |
| 12 | 69.3 | 64.4 |
| 10 | 68.3 | 63.4 |
| 8 | 67.0 | 63.3 |
| 6 | 63.9 | 60.7 |
| 4 | 58.7 | 58.9 |
